slides.title: Helping Volunteers Stay and Grow
slides.sub: Why do good volunteers quietly disappear?

slides.title: You will learn
list: Why recruiting is the easy part
How Jesus trained people: brief, send, debrief
One conversation that will do more for your team than any appeal
slides.narration: In this lesson you will learn why recruiting is the easy part, how Jesus trained people by sending them out and then debriefing them, and one conversation that will do more for your team than any appeal from the front.

slides.quote: “And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers, to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ.”
slides.narration:
Let’s begin with Scripture. Ephesians chapter 4, verses 11 and 12.

"And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers, to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ."

slides.title: Katartismos: to mend, to fit, to prepare
body: The word for mending nets and setting a broken bone. Leaders are given to equip people, not to use them.
slides.sub: Preparing people to participate, not keeping ministry in the hands of a few.
slides.narration:
Paul is writing to the church in Ephesus about how Christ has structured his body. And notice what leaders are for. They are given to equip the saints for the work of ministry. The emphasis is on preparing people to participate, not on keeping ministry in the hands of a few.

The word translated "equip" is katartismos. It comes from a verb used in Mark 1 for James and John mending their nets, and it was used by physicians for setting a broken bone. It means to restore something to working order, to fit it for its purpose. That is your job description with volunteers. Not to use them. To mend, fit and prepare them, so that they can serve well.

slides.title: A retention problem that looks like a recruitment problem
body: They serve for a few months, drift to the back of the rota, and quietly stop. Nobody has a conversation about it.
slides.sub: Three preventable causes: unclear expectations, thanks that never landed, no growth.
slides.narration:
Now here is what actually happens in most ministries. People say yes, serve for a few months, drift to the back of the rota, and then quietly stop. Nobody has a conversation about it. The leader concludes the church is uncommitted, and starts asking for volunteers again. A ministry can look as if it has a recruitment problem when it really has a retention problem.

People leave for many good reasons: work, health, caring responsibilities, a move, a change of calling. But three preventable problems deserve your attention. They never knew exactly what was expected. Nobody ever said thank you in a way that landed. And they stopped growing: year three looked exactly like year one, and nobody asked what they wanted to become.

slides.title: Brief, send in pairs, debrief
body: Jesus sent the Twelve out two by two with concrete instructions. When they came back, they gathered around him and reported everything.
slides.sub: He debriefed the people, not just the results.
slides.narration:
Look at how Jesus did it. Mark 6 says he called the Twelve and began to send them out two by two. He did not send them alone, and he did not send them empty-handed. Matthew 10 records the briefing he gave first: where to go, what to say, what to take, what to do when a town would not receive them. Then Mark 6:30 records what happened when they came back. The apostles gathered around Jesus and reported to him all they had done and taught. That is the pattern. Brief, send in pairs, debrief.

And when the seventy-two came back in Luke 10, thrilled that even the demons submitted to them, Jesus did not dismiss the joy. He redirected it: do not rejoice that the spirits submit to you, rejoice that your names are written in heaven. He debriefed the people, not just the results. He was interested in what serving was doing to them. Most of us send volunteers out with a vague description and never ask how it went. Then we wonder why they fade.

slides.title: Recruiting someone is the beginning of leadership, not the end.
body: If your only contact with your volunteers is about their tasks, you have a rota, not a team.
slides.narration: So here is the truth for this lesson. Recruiting someone is the beginning of leadership, not the end. If your only contact with your volunteers is about their tasks, you have a rota, not a team.

slides.title: Which volunteer is most at risk of quietly fading in the next three months?
body: What is actually going on with them? Take a moment before you go on.
slides.narration: So pause here for a moment. Name the volunteer most at risk of quietly fading out in the next three months. What is actually going on with them? Take a moment before you go on.

slides.title: The four training steps
slides.sub: Delegate the outcome, not just the task. Safety, accuracy and money are never optional standards.
slides.narration:
Here is the tool for this week. It has two parts.

The first is the training sequence that actually transfers a skill. Four steps. I do it, you watch: explain what you are doing as you go, including the small judgement calls. We do it together. You do it, I watch: they lead, you say nothing unless something is going badly wrong, and you give feedback afterwards, privately. And finally, you do it, I’m available: you step out. You are reachable, but you are not standing there. Most leaders jump from step one to step four and call it delegation. The person fails, the leader takes the job back, and both conclude the volunteer wasn’t up to it. And when you do hand something over, delegate the outcome, not just the task. "Make sure the room feels welcoming by nine-thirty" produces someone who notices the heating is off and fixes it. "Put out forty chairs" produces someone who puts out chairs. Agree the outcome, the limits and the standard first. Safety, accuracy and the responsible handling of money are never optional standards.

slides.title: The six-month review
list: What part of this do you most enjoy?
Do you want to continue, change, or stop?
slides.narration: The second part is the review. Every role should have a review date, the six-month point from last week’s invitation. At the review, ask three questions and mean all three. What part of this do you most enjoy? What part drains you? Do you want to continue, change, or stop? Make "stop" a genuinely acceptable answer. A volunteer who leaves well, thanked and blessed, tells other people that serving here is a good experience. A volunteer who leaves by disappearing tells them the opposite. And when someone isn’t working out, never let a reliability or attitude problem run for months without a direct conversation. Consider whether a different role would fit better. But concerns about abuse, dishonesty or unsafe conduct go through the appropriate process. You do not transfer that kind of problem to another team.

slides.title: One unhurried conversation. No task agenda.
body: Tell them beforehand you want to hear how serving is affecting them. Ask what they enjoy, what has been difficult, and whether anything is affecting their capacity. Then thank them for one specific thing.
slides.note: If they want to stop, receive it without guilt or pressure.
slides.narration: So this is your step. Take the person you thought of a moment ago, and invite them to an unhurried conversation this week, in an appropriate setting, with no agenda about tasks. Tell them beforehand that you want to hear how serving is affecting them, not to assess their performance. Ask three things: what do you enjoy about serving? What has been difficult or draining? And, is there anything affecting your capacity that you would like me to know? Let them share only what they are comfortable sharing, and listen without trying to solve everything. Then thank them for one specific thing you have watched them do. Name the action, and name why it mattered. And if they tell you they want to stop, receive that without guilt or pressure. That single conversation will do more for your team than anything else in this lesson.

slides.title: You have a team when you know the people, not just the rota.
slides.narration: One truth to carry with you this week. You have a team when you know the people, not just the rota.

body: Lord, you sent your disciples out and then sat with them when they came back. Teach me to do the same. Help me to notice the person who is quietly fading, to thank people in ways that land, and to equip rather than use the people you have given me. Build up your body through this team. Amen.
slides.narration:
Let me close with a short prayer.

Lord, you sent your disciples out and then sat with them when they came back. Teach me to do the same. Help me to notice the person who is quietly fading, to thank people in ways that land, and to equip rather than use the people you have given me. Build up your body through this team. Amen.
